## 14. Stopped-sim services
- V1 §9.6 previewed trim and linearization as clients of an activation (the build's typed products at a given scalar type). [§9.6]
- V2 The stopped-sim services are initialization, trim, linearization, and `checkpoint` with its partner `restore!`.
- V3 The first three share one artifact, the condition.
- V4 A condition is the datum that says "set this build to this state." `checkpoint` returns a checkpoint (the `Model`'s state at a frame top as one value), and `restore!` puts it back.
- V5 A checkpoint is a distinct value with no condition algebra (D-273). [D-273]
- V6 §14.1 settles the condition's representation, §14.2 its composition, §14.3 its resolution and §14.4 its application; §14.5 covers the boundary-zero sequence; §14.6 covers root-input totality (the requirement that an application establishing a complete world cover every root input); §14.7 the trim problem, §14.8 the trim service and §14.9 mounting, which together cover the trim service in full; and §14.10 covers linearization. [§14.1, §14.2, §14.3, §14.4, §14.5, §14.6, §14.7, §14.8, §14.9, §14.10]

#### Lifecycle preconditions
- V7 Every service requires a non-running simulation (D-108). [D-108] (bold)
- V8 While a run exists the loop owns the stores between drains (the frame-top swap that publishes staged device writes into the root inputs), and a service reading or writing them would race it.
- V9 Pause is no exception, by the doctrine that freezes the roster (the list of attached devices, read once at `run!`).
- V10 Pause is a control-plane state inside a run, so a prohibition that holds mid-run holds while paused (§11.3, §12.1). [§11.3, §12.1]

### 14.1 Conditions are path-addressed overlays on the declared defaults
- V53 This section covers, in order, what a condition may specify, the overlay base, why addressing a condition by path is legitimate, the pre-sweep doctrine and the environment queries a condition may make.
- V54 A condition may specify state fields, `x` on the continuous tier and `s` on the discrete.
- V55 It may also specify modes, `m`, which only continuous components have (§3.2). [§3.2]
- V56 All three are addressed by a slash path (§8.6) plus a field name. [§8.6]
- V57 Beyond state, a condition may specify root inputs, addressed by face (the name a port wears on its component's boundary).
- V58 It never specifies outputs, which are derived data (D-063). [D-063] (bold)
- V59 It never specifies workspace (component-declared mutable scratch arriving as the `ws` bundle field) (D-306). [D-306]
- V60 Condition entries are validated in the collecting form (§13.1). [§13.1]
- V61 The full list is checked, violations are collected, and one `DiagnosticError` is thrown.
- V62 A condition entry naming an output or a workspace field is one such violation, `ConditionResolution` with reason `:undeclared_field` (Appendix C). [Appendix C]
- V63 The overlay base is always the declared defaults (D-063). [D-063] (bold)
- V64 Every store (the framework-owned home of a component's `x`, `s` or `m` state) has a declared initial value under declaration-by-initial-value (§8.2), so conditions are naturally sparse. [§8.2]
- V65 Applying one means "fresh run from the `x_init`, `s_init` and `m_init` defaults, with these overrides" (D-063). [D-063]
- V66 A condition is an initial condition and nothing else (D-273). [D-273] (bold)
- V67 A simulation's state past its initial instant is a checkpoint (the `Model`'s state at a frame top as one value), not a condition, and it has no algebra (D-274). [D-274]
- V68 Addressing conditions by path does not reopen the observation-by-path rejection (§13.5, D-409). [§13.5, D-409]
- V69 That rejection bars a run from acting on reads its model did not declare.
- V70 A condition is not such a read.
- V71 It is a design-time statement about a concrete build, written before the run begins, and the locality law of §14.2 is how an author keeps it to children the author owns. [§14.2]
- V72 A would-be init value that depends on swept outputs is either analytically known to the caller or an equilibrium constraint (D-064). [D-064] (bold)
- V73 This is the pre-sweep doctrine, and it holds because condition writes precede the first sweep (one pass through the execution order against the current state) by definition.
- V74 The first case is trim's `α_filt = α_a`.
- V75 There α is a decision variable, so the value is known above, not computable below.
- V76 The second case is a job for the trim service, not for init.
- V77 "Caller-computable" reaches past closed-form knowledge to environment queries (D-139). [D-139] (bold)
- V78 A condition needing one constructs the same handle the sweep will produce, and then calls the same query function the consuming component calls.
- V79 There are two routes to that handle.
- V80 One is the value-level constructor (the plain public function building a field handle from the component and input values) of §8.2, applied to the same values the `baseline` writes into the environment component's root inputs. [§8.2]
- V81 The other applies in a rig where an isbits handle itself is a root-input value (§4.4, D-364). [§4.4, D-364]
- V82 There the condition simply holds the value the `baseline` wrote.
- V83 Either way there is one implementation of the field math, evaluated one level up, with no pre-sweep and no new mechanism.
- V84 Where closed-form enforcement of a target is not wanted at all, the second escape already covers the case (D-139). [D-139]
- V85 Promote the eliminated state coordinates to decision variables and enforce the targets as residuals on swept outputs.
- V86 That route needs no environment access at condition time whatsoever.

### 14.2 Fragment composition: locality without schema
- V87 Init knowledge is component-local.
- V88 An engine component knows `n_eng → ω = n_eng·ω_rated`, and nothing above it should have to.
- V89 Making that locality a schema entry was rejected (D-064). [D-064]
- V90 That spelling would declare `initialize(::C, spec)`, a declarative rebirth of `f_init!`, FlightCore's per-model initialization hook.
- V91 It would also add an assembly-level rule routing sub-specs to children.
- V92 This section covers, in order, the condition method, composition by pull, what `set`'s payloads may name, the inert tree, the empty-prefix refusal, the locality law, and the collision and blend errors.
- V93 What preserves the locality is an idiom, not schema (D-064). [D-064] (bold)
- V94 It is the condition method, a method of the framework's `condition` generic, shipped beside the component and dispatched on the component, returning the component's own fragment (the leaf node of the condition algebra, built by `set`) (D-405). [D-405]
- V95 The generic is framework-owned so that an owner's pull, described below, reaches a child's fragment when the two live in different packages.
- V96 A model package extends it through `import Redstone: condition`, as it extends the declaration family (§8.1). [§8.1]
- V97 No shadowing check covers it.
- V98 A method written to a foreign `condition` fails loudly at the owner's pull, as a `MethodError` naming the child (D-316). [D-316]
- V99 In the first block, the engine is an illustrative component named after FlightPhysics' `PistonEngine`, and `Phase` an illustrative enum of its modes.
- V100 [code block] condition(eng::PistonEngine; n_eng) =
- V101 Fragments are composed by pull from the structure's owner, here `C172XSystems` (the C172X aircraft's systems assembly, after FlightApps' `C172X.Systems`).
- V102 [code block] condition(sys::C172XSystems; n_eng, α_a, β_a) = combine(
- V103 `set`'s payloads speak only about the component at the authoring point.
- V104 Addressing children is exclusively the job of `at` (the scoping combinator), so there is one way to say everything.
- V105 A `u` payload names faces of the authoring level's contract.
- V106 Resolution walks the export chain to the root input and errors if the face never surfaces (D-065), as `ConditionResolution` with reason `:no_input_face`, or `:unexported_face` at the root (Appendix C). [D-065, Appendix C] (bold)
- V107 That walk always has a name to follow.
- V108 One-level routing gives every level a declared face for every signal crossing its boundary, so the chain a sub-assembly's face routes through is in the `Build` (§6.1, §9.2, D-207). [§6.1, §9.2, D-207]
- V109 An internally-wired input has no root input behind it, and writing it would be meaningless because the first sweep overwrites it.
- V110 Such a write is `ConditionResolution` with reason `:internally_wired`.
- V111 Unexported stays unpokeable for init exactly as it is for a front end's panels (§11.7). [§11.7]
- V112 Dispatch selects variant-specific methods, so the actuation split between FlightApps' C172 variants, c172s and c172x, costs no upstream edits.
- V113 Composition builds an inert, lazy fragment tree (D-065). [D-065] (bold)
- V114 `set` builds the leaf, and `at` and `combine` (the symmetric, collision-intolerant combinator) build the tree's inner nodes.
- V115 No path arithmetic happens at composition.
- V116 [code block] struct Fragment{X,S,M,L}  x::X; s::S; m::M; u::L  end      #set(; x, s, m, u): self-vocabulary payloads; no paths
- V117 Every node is isbits except the prefix strings, and a prefix is a reference to the author's own literal.
- V118 So, with literal prefixes, rebuilding the tree per trim iteration allocates nothing.
- V119 There is no path arithmetic and no copy of the payloads.
- V120 Composition checks three things, each by type or length alone, and none allocates.
- V121 Each `set` payload is a NamedTuple, each combinator operand is a node, and each `at` prefix is nonempty.
- V122 A `set` payload that is not a NamedTuple is `ConditionNodeMisuse` with reason `:set_payload` (Appendix C). [Appendix C]
- V123 The trim of Flight.jl's Cessna 172 model (`c172.jl`) writes each trial state through FlightPhysics' `assign!`, and the zero-alloc property of that `assign!` loop holds of the construction and of the specialized `apply!` that writes the tree (§14.4) alike. [§14.4]
- V124 An evaluation's cost is therefore the sweep it feeds.
- V125 `at` refuses an empty prefix when it is called (D-278). [D-278] (bold)
- V126 An empty prefix names no child, and a node meant for the level where it is authored stays unwrapped.
- V127 The refusal holds at the root too, because `at` builds an inert tree and cannot know where it will be mounted.
- V128 On a condition node it raises `ConditionNodeMisuse` with reason `:empty_prefix` (Appendix C) before any resolution pass runs. [Appendix C]
- V129 The read side's lifts refuse the same way (§14.9, D-278). [§14.9, D-278]
- V130 The locality law here is the one §6.1 states for connections, now in its third instance (D-065). [§6.1, D-065] (bold)
- V131 The three instances are local wires, computed interface connections and conditions.
- V132 Each level speaks its own fields, its declared children's names, and its own faces.
- V133 Delegation runs by dispatch at every genericity seam (D-064). [D-064]
- V134 An `at` prefix may stop at any child's faces, owned or generically held, because the face graph is total (D-207). [D-207]
- V135 A deep `at` or condition path resolves wherever the structure has it (§13.3, D-414). [§13.3, D-414]
- V136 Absolute paths exist only in the flattened list of condition entries, a compiled derivative of the composition, as cell offsets are of `local_wires`.
- V137 Under the locality law, substituting a component invalidates only the fragments its owner shipped.
- V138 The build checks the law wherever it can see what the law constrains.
- V139 Wiring resolves one level (§6.1). [§6.1]
- V140 The faces a `u` payload names resolve through the export chain, under any `at` prefix (D-207). [D-207]
- V141 No check refuses a deep path past a generically held field (D-414). [D-414]
- V142 An author who ships a fragment for a family scopes it by dispatch on the holding's type parameter, so a fragment reaching into one powerplant is defined for the aircraft that hold that powerplant (D-414). [D-414]
- V143 Ownership alone is convention.
- V144 It is a fact about who maintains the code, and the build cannot see it, so keeping a deep path inside an owned subtree is idiomatic rather than machine-checked (D-065). [D-065]
- V145 `set`, `at` and `combine` are ordinary functions with no privileges, as the blocks of §13.7 are ordinary components. [§13.7]
- V146 A `combine` collision is two condition entries on one leaf.
- V147 Collisions are errors at resolution (D-065). [D-065] (bold)
- V148 The error is `DuplicateConditionLeaf` (Appendix C), and it reports both origins. [Appendix C]
- V149 Its message names the layering combinator, "`combine` is collision-intolerant by design — use `override(base, patch)` to layer." Last-writer-wins was rejected (D-065). [D-065]
- V150 That rejection is also why the combinator is not `Base.merge`, and is no longer named after it (D-204). [D-204] (bold)
- V151 `Base.merge` is last-wins on NamedTuples, the exact semantics rejected here, and its own name should not promise them.
- V152 Because `combine` is its own function, a bare NamedTuple blended into a node cannot fall through to any last-wins method.
- V153 The blend is still closed explicitly.
- V154 A `combine(::Fragment, ::NamedTuple)`, or any other blend of a condition node with a bare NamedTuple, is an error method.
- V155 Its message is directive.
- V156 It says to wrap the NamedTuple in `set(…)` (or `at(prefix, set(…))`) and to combine nodes with nodes.
- V157 The rejection carries a kind like every other.
- V158 It is `ConditionNodeMisuse` (Appendix C, D-113), carrying the offending argument's type and the node kinds in hand. [Appendix C, D-113] (bold)
- V159 It is raised at composition time, before any resolution pass runs or any origin exists.
- V160 That is why it is its own kind and not a `ConditionResolution` sub-kind (§14.3). [§14.3]
- V161 The explicit, ordered layering spelling, `override`, belongs with the use case root-input totality produces (§14.6). [§14.6]

### 14.3 Resolution: flatten, validate, compile once
- V162 Resolution takes the root node plus a `Build` (the artifact `build(world)` produces).
- V163 This section covers, in order, flattening, the collecting checks, the two lookup families, the plan, the converter rule with its two cases, and overlay partiality.
- V164 Flattening is the only place path strings are ever concatenated (D-065). [D-065] (bold)
- V165 It is a trivial recursion with a path accumulator, and it also records each condition entry's tree position, its `getfield`/`getindex` step tuple.
- V166 The collecting pass then checks each flat condition entry:
- V167 the path resolves, with did-you-mean (the offending name plus the list-in-hand it should have matched) over children;
- V168 the field is declared in the target's `x_init`/`s_init`/`m_init`;
- V169 the value type is convertible to the declared leaf type;
- V170 input faces reach root inputs;
- V171 no leaf is written twice, where a `u` payload's leaf is the root input its face resolves to.
- V172 Each check names its kind (Appendix C). [Appendix C]
- V173 A path that does not resolve is `PathResolution` with reason `:unknown_child`.
- V174 An undeclared field is `ConditionResolution` with reason `:undeclared_field`, or `:no_store` or `:assembly_path` where the target has no such store or is an assembly.
- V175 A value that does not convert is `ConditionResolution` with reason `:unconvertible`.
- V176 A face that reaches no root input takes one of the face reasons §14.2 names. [§14.2]
- V177 A leaf written twice is `DuplicateConditionLeaf`.
- V178 The `Build` supplies two lookup families.
- V179 Schema is the evaluated declarations, and it is the authority.
- V180 It answers whether you may write this field, and at what leaf type.
- V181 Layout is the destination.
- V182 It holds the `x` backing ranges, the store indices for `s` and for `m`, and the root-input indices from the activation (the build's typed products at a given scalar type).
- V183 The face chains come from `Structure` (the structure step's product, the components, wires, faces and tiers), never from an activation's typing; the names a declaration evaluates to are the same at every activation (§9.1, D-253). [§9.1, D-253]
- V184 A valid list of condition entries compiles two ways (§14.4). [§14.4]
- V185 The specialized `apply!`'s plan holds, per leaf, a lens (the compiled navigation step of a condition entry), a destination and a converter.
- V186 The lens is the position tuple lifted to a type parameter, so navigation of the fixed tree type is type-stable.
- V187 The converter is baked now, selected per leaf from that leaf's type in the resolved shape (D-065, D-148). [D-065, D-148] (bold)
- V188 Leaf types are shape facts, carried by the tree type along with the full nesting and every field name (§14.4). [§14.4]
- V189 Selection therefore consults no runtime fact and stays a resolution-time bake.
- V190 There are two cases.
- V191 already at the activation's scalar type, decision-descended
- V192 the type's ordinary `convert`/constructor methods at that eltype
- V193 a plain `Float64` leaf against a non-nominal activation's scratch, a held constant
- V194 the `Float64 → Dual` zero-partial embedding
- V195 A leaf already at the activation's scalar type is decision-descended.
- V196 Under a `Dual`-seeded evaluation of a type-stable `trim_condition(d)`, every decision-dependent leaf is `Dual`-typed in the shape (§14.7). [§14.7]
- V197 Such a leaf takes the type's ordinary `convert`/constructor methods at that eltype.
- V198 An authored `RQuat` (FlightPhysics' rotation quaternion) of `Dual`s becomes the `SVector{4}` state leaf at `Dual`, with the partials flowing through untouched.
- V199 That untouched flow of partials is what makes the seeded decisions reach the sweep at all.
- V200 At the nominal activation the same rule is the ordinary `Float64` conversion.
- V201 An authored `RQuat` value becomes the `SVector{4}` state leaf it initializes.
- V202 A plain `Float64` leaf against a non-nominal activation's scratch is a held constant, and it takes the `Float64 → Dual` zero-partial embedding.
- V203 That embedding is semantically exact in that case, and in no other.
- V204 "Held at the operating point" is zero partials.
- V205 Zero partials are the whole of a linearization operating-point condition, which is authored decision-free (§14.10). [§14.10]
- V206 The selection is a one-time resolution decision, and it leaves the nominal exact-match doctrine for table cells (§9.5) untouched. [§9.5]
- V207 Converters run here, on the write path.
- V208 They never run on state views (§7.1, D-148). [§7.1, D-148]
- V209 Overlay partiality for the `s` and `m` stores is baked the same way (D-065). [D-065]
- V210 Each `s` or `m` store's write is one whole value, `merge(defaults, overlay)`, with the store's declared defaults resolved at compile time under the overlay-base rule (§14.1). [§14.1]
